Image Processing · Lab 12 · Material

Photometric Augmentation

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Explore controlled changes to the appearance of familiar tabletop objects. You will inspect both the pictures and the numeric limits before proposing a training policy.

What you will learn

  • Apply brightness, contrast and saturation changes without integer wraparound.
  • Distinguish random noise, blur and compression effects.
  • Use paired comparisons and recorded parameters.
  • Reject appearance changes that invalidate the target meaning.

Before this lab: Use RGB uint8 and float arrays, image histograms and local random generators.

In this lab

  1. Brightness and Clipping
  2. Contrast Around a Stated Pivot
  3. Saturation and Color Evidence
  4. Seeded Additive Noise
  5. Blur Severity and Useful Detail
  6. Compression as a Round Trip
  7. Paired Severity Comparisons
  8. Plausible Appearance Policies

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Drawn fixtures are RGB uint8 in H,W,C order. Convert to float before arithmetic; display uint8 [0,255] or float [0,1].

Python · shared setup
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from io import BytesIO
import numpy as np
import cv2
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(212)

# Drawn tabletop fixtures: RGB uint8, H=128, W=160, C=3.
def scene(kind="mug", seed=0):
    local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:128, :160]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(xx / 3) + local.normal(0, 1, (128, 160))
    base = np.stack([205 + yy / 8 + grain, 191 + yy / 10 + grain,
                     166 + yy / 12 + grain], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(base, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    for y in range(12, 128, 24):
        draw.line((0, y, 159, y), fill=(184, 168, 146), width=1)
    if kind == "mug":
        draw.ellipse((105, 43, 139, 87), fill=(53, 118, 167))
        draw.ellipse((112, 50, 131, 80), fill=(208, 193, 168))
        draw.rounded_rectangle((43, 33, 115, 102), radius=12, fill=(66, 145, 194))
        draw.ellipse((43, 27, 115, 48), fill=(34, 71, 91))
        draw.ellipse((48, 31, 110, 43), fill=(116, 71, 40))
        draw.text((64, 64), "TEA", fill=(245, 246, 237))
    elif kind == "parcel":
        draw.rectangle((27, 31, 123, 101), fill=(174, 117, 65), outline=(70, 45, 28), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((69, 32, 80, 100), fill=(224, 190, 124))
        draw.rectangle((86, 48, 115, 77), fill=(247, 244, 225))
        draw.text((89, 55), "UP", fill=(25, 30, 34))
        draw.line((39, 64, 39, 45), fill=(25, 30, 34), width=3)
        draw.polygon([(33, 48), (45, 48), (39, 41)], fill=(25, 30, 34))
    elif kind == "apple":
        draw.ellipse((43, 38, 115, 108), fill=(190, 48, 40))
        draw.ellipse((58, 44, 75, 63), fill=(241, 123, 93))
        draw.line((80, 42, 86, 26), fill=(75, 63, 32), width=5)
        draw.ellipse((84, 25, 104, 35), fill=(54, 117, 56))
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unknown fixture kind")
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()

def panels(images, titles, cmap=None):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(images), figsize=(4 * len(images), 3.4), squeeze=False)
    for ax, image, title in zip(axes[0], images, titles):
        ax.imshow(image, cmap=cmap)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.axis("off")
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Brightness and Clipping

An additive brightness offset shifts every RGB channel by the same amount. Work in floating point first: adding directly to uint8 can wrap large values into dark values before you have a chance to clip. Our operation is round(clip(image + offset, 0, 255)). Rounding explicitly makes the conversion rule visible, although this first integer offset does not need fractional rounding.

Count channel values that would fall outside the legal range before clipping. That count is different from the number of saturated pixels: one pixel can contribute up to three channel values. Clipping loses distinctions between values beyond the boundary, so subtracting the offset afterwards cannot generally recover the original. This is a useful numeric audit, not an exposure measurement in physical light units. The drawn RGB values are display-encoded intensities, and this simple offset is an appearance augmentation.

Try it

  1. Convert a mug image to float32.
  2. Add 35 and clip before converting back.
  3. Measure the fraction of channel values clipped.
Python · run in order
image = scene("mug")
raw = image.astype(np.float32) + 35.0
clipped_fraction = float(np.mean((raw < 0) | (raw > 255)))
brighter = np.rint(np.clip(raw, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8)
fig = panels([image, brighter], ["Original", f"Offset +35; clipped {clipped_fraction:.1%}"])

Read the result

Look at the pale printed letters and bright table regions. Their loss of tonal separation can matter to a reading task even if the mug outline remains clear. The measured fraction describes this array and this offset only.

Change and compare

  • Try an offset of −35 and count lower-bound clipping.
  • Compare channel-value clipping with pixels having at least one clipped channel.

Guided task 02

Contrast Around a Stated Pivot

Contrast needs a pivot as well as a factor. We use 127.5 on the 0–255 scale and compute pivot + factor × (image − pivot). A factor below one pulls channel values toward the pivot, while a factor above one pushes them away. This fixed-pivot operation differs from centering each picture around its own mean; two implementations with the same factor can therefore produce different images.

Compare factors 0.65 and 1.35 with identical rounding and clipping rules. Keep the pivot recorded with the factor so a replay has a complete definition. The operation acts independently on RGB channel values and can affect color appearance as well as brightness separation. A histogram could show the changed spread, but the actual picture is needed to judge whether small printed details remain visible. Larger numeric spread is not proof of a more useful future model input.

Try it

  1. Set a fixed pivot of 127.5.
  2. Apply low and high contrast factors in floating point.
  3. Use the same clipping rule for both outputs.
Python · run in order
pivot = 127.5
factors = [0.65, 1.35]
contrasts = [np.rint(np.clip(pivot + factor * (image.astype(np.float32) - pivot), 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8) for factor in factors]
fig = panels([image] + contrasts, ["Original", "Contrast 0.65", "Contrast 1.35"])

Read the result

The low-contrast picture is pulled toward mid-gray; the high-contrast result can push highlights or shadows against a boundary. Compare the word on the cup and the tabletop grain rather than judging only the most saturated region.

Change and compare

  • Repeat with pivot 100 and explain why the result differs.
  • Apply factor one and check exact recovery of the uint8 input.

Guided task 03

Saturation and Color Evidence

Saturation adjusts color intensity without deliberately changing hue. Convert our uint8 RGB array with COLOR_RGB2HSV; explicit RGB arrays are not automatically BGR just because OpenCV processes them. In this uint8 HSV representation, hue uses 0–179 and saturation and value use 0–255. The float HSV convention is different, so do not mix numeric ranges between the two representations.

Scale only the saturation channel in floating point, clip it, convert back to uint8, then return to RGB. A zero factor produces a grayscale-looking result through HSV, while a modest factor below one reduces colorfulness. The meaning still depends on the target. Apple-versus-mug identity may tolerate less saturation, but a target that distinguishes red from green fruit depends on color evidence. Even a spatially perfect transform can erase information needed by the original label.

Try it

  1. Convert an apple from RGB to uint8 HSV.
  2. Change saturation only for factors 0 and 0.65.
  3. Convert both results back to RGB for display.
Python · run in order
apple = scene("apple")
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(apple, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
saturation_views = []
for factor in [0.0, 0.65]:
    altered = hsv.copy()
    altered[..., 1] = np.rint(np.clip(hsv[..., 1].astype(np.float32) * factor, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8)
    saturation_views.append(cv2.cvtColor(altered, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB))
fig = panels([apple] + saturation_views, ["Original RGB", "Saturation 0", "Saturation 0.65"])

Read the result

Color removal leaves edges and shape coordinates intact but changes the available evidence. Small round-trip RGB differences are possible because conversion uses finite precision; an HSV round trip is not a lossless file codec.

Change and compare

  • Check the grayscale-looking result's three channels for equality.
  • Discuss which factors are acceptable when the label includes fruit color.

Guided task 04

Seeded Additive Noise

Noise augmentation can represent limited appearance variability without claiming to reproduce a particular camera. Here each channel receives an independent Gaussian sample with mean zero and standard deviation 12 on the 0–255 scale. Generate the noise in floating point, add it to the image, and clip only at the output boundary. A local seed makes this specific noisy view reproducible.

Zero-mean sampled noise does not guarantee exactly zero mean over a finite array. Clipping near zero or 255 can also shift the mean of the final pixel differences. Examine a magnified crop so the noise is visible without confusing it with a changed object position. This implementation adds independent color-channel noise; a single H-by-W noise field broadcast over channels would model another appearance pattern. Neither construction is a complete physical sensor model.

Try it

  1. Sample a full H,W,3 noise array with seed 612.
  2. Add standard deviation 12 noise before clipping.
  3. Display the full output and a detailed crop.
Python · run in order
noise_rng = np.random.default_rng(612)
noise = noise_rng.normal(0, 12, image.shape).astype(np.float32)
noisy = np.rint(np.clip(image.astype(np.float32) + noise, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8)
fig = panels([image, noisy, noisy[48:88, 55:105]], ["Original", "Independent RGB noise", "Detail crop"])

Read the result

The crop exposes the grain added to smooth regions and the printed letters. Subtract in a signed or floating representation when measuring differences; uint8 subtraction would corrupt negative changes through wraparound.

Change and compare

  • Compute the mean signed final difference and compare it with noise.mean().
  • Broadcast one two-dimensional noise field across RGB and compare its appearance.

Guided task 05

Blur Severity and Useful Detail

Blur combines nearby pixels, reducing fine detail as well as noise. GaussianBlur accepts an odd kernel size and a standard deviation; record both rather than calling an output simply “blurred”. Here we compare a 3-by-3 kernel with sigma 0.6 against a 9-by-9 kernel with sigma 2.0, keeping the same reflected-border rule.

The parcel's arrow and letters make the semantic cost visible. A coarse object-identity task might tolerate some softening, while reading small print may fail long before the rectangle disappears. Large blur is therefore a stress test, not automatically a stronger or better augmentation. The output remains RGB uint8 with the same geometry, yet the amount of usable evidence changes. Comparing actual details supports a reasoned policy bound; it does not establish how a future classifier will behave.

Try it

  1. Apply mild and stronger Gaussian kernels.
  2. Use BORDER_REFLECT_101 explicitly.
  3. Compare the printed label and arrow in all views.
Python · run in order
parcel = scene("parcel")
mild_blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(parcel, (3, 3), 0.6, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
strong_blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(parcel, (9, 9), 2.0, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
fig = panels([parcel, mild_blur, strong_blur], ["Original", "3x3, sigma 0.6", "9x9, sigma 2.0"])

Read the result

The two outputs retain the same coordinates but differ in local information. Inspect the smaller label rather than only the large outline; the first feature to disappear may be precisely the one required by a task.

Change and compare

  • Inspect identical crops of the printed UP in all three arrays.
  • Try a constant-color input to separate blur behavior from object detail.

Guided task 06

Compression as a Round Trip

JPEG augmentation means encoding and decoding an actual image, not adding an arbitrary block pattern and calling it compression. Use an in-memory BytesIO buffer so no source files are overwritten. Pillow receives our RGB array, saves JPEG with an explicit quality and chroma-subsampling setting, then decodes back to RGB. The encoder quality scale is a parameter, not a percentage of retained image quality.

Compare qualities 90 and 20 with subsampling fixed at zero so this experiment changes one encoder setting. File size and reconstruction error can be measured for these exact drawings, but they do not determine recognition accuracy. Printed edges and textured regions are useful places to inspect artifacts. A decoded JPEG still has the same height and width; matching dimensions do not imply matching pixel values. Preserve the untouched source when investigating lossy encodings.

Try it

  1. Encode the parcel at two quality settings in memory.
  2. Decode both payloads as RGB arrays.
  3. Inspect detail and retain payload byte counts.
Python · run in order
decoded = []
byte_counts = []
for quality in [90, 20]:
    buffer = BytesIO()
    Image.fromarray(parcel).save(buffer, format="JPEG", quality=quality, subsampling=0)
    payload = buffer.getvalue()
    byte_counts.append(len(payload))
    with Image.open(BytesIO(payload)) as opened:
        decoded.append(np.asarray(opened.convert("RGB")).copy())
fig = panels([parcel] + decoded, ["Original", f"JPEG 90: {byte_counts[0]} bytes", f"JPEG 20: {byte_counts[1]} bytes"])

Read the result

Look near text and high-contrast tape edges for actual codec artifacts. The byte counts are measurements of these encoded fixtures and settings; another image can have different size and error at the same nominal quality.

Change and compare

  • Measure mean absolute RGB error using float subtraction.
  • Change subsampling while holding quality fixed and inspect colored edges.

Guided task 07

Paired Severity Comparisons

When comparing severity, control unrelated randomness. Drawing independent noise for two different standard deviations changes both the pattern and its scale, making local visual comparisons harder. Instead draw one standard-normal field and multiply it by two specified values. This common-noise construction isolates the effect of scale for the paired demonstration.

The two outputs are still clipped independently, so their final differences are not guaranteed to be exact multiples near the numeric boundaries. The shared field belongs to an inspection experiment; a training pipeline may appropriately draw a new field for every request. State which behavior you intend. Keep the original array, sampled field and parameters separate so you can reconstruct a comparison and investigate surprising pixels without relying only on screenshots.

Try it

  1. Generate one standard-normal field with seed 712.
  2. Use scales 5 and 18 on that same field.
  3. Compare the outputs and an absolute-difference image.
Python · run in order
paired_rng = np.random.default_rng(712)
unit_noise = paired_rng.standard_normal(apple.shape).astype(np.float32)
low_noise = np.rint(np.clip(apple.astype(np.float32) + 5 * unit_noise, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8)
high_noise = np.rint(np.clip(apple.astype(np.float32) + 18 * unit_noise, 0, 255)).astype(np.uint8)
difference = np.abs(high_noise.astype(np.float32) - low_noise.astype(np.float32)).mean(axis=2)
fig = panels([low_noise, high_noise, difference], ["Shared field: sigma 5", "Shared field: sigma 18", "Mean absolute RGB difference"])
difference_axis = fig.axes[-1]
difference_axis.images[0].set_clim(vmin=0)
fig.colorbar(difference_axis.images[0],ax=difference_axis,label="Mean absolute channel difference")
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The difference image measures channel changes between two controlled outputs; it is not a probability map or an object mask. Clipped highlights can respond differently from midrange pixels even under the same sampled field.

Change and compare

  • Add scale zero as a baseline and verify exact input recovery.
  • Repeat with independent fields to identify what the paired design controls.

Guided task 08

Plausible Appearance Policies

A policy is a bounded recipe with a stated purpose. For this example, we propose modest contrast in [0.9,1.1] followed by brightness in [−15,15] for mug identity. Sample both parameters, apply the operations in floating point, and clip once at the end. The output is a candidate to inspect, not evidence of improved generalization. If reading the printed word were the target, the same bounds would need a separate review.

Also construct an exaggerated comparison with contrast 2.5 and offset 90. Its role is to reveal why clipping and evidence checks belong in policy selection. Record the pre-clipping fraction for both outputs and examine which features disappear. Do not choose policy strength by repeatedly looking at a held-out test set. Use domain requirements and training-side inspection to propose candidates, reserve validation for controlled selection later, and leave test evaluation untouched.

Try it

  1. Sample modest factors using seed 812.
  2. Apply contrast then brightness with one final clip.
  3. Compare against a clearly marked stress configuration.
Python · run in order
policy_rng = np.random.default_rng(812)
parameters = {"contrast": float(policy_rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1)), "offset": float(policy_rng.uniform(-15, 15))}
candidate_raw = 127.5 + parameters["contrast"] * (image.astype(np.float32)-127.5) + parameters["offset"]
stress_raw = 127.5 + 2.5 * (image.astype(np.float32)-127.5) + 90
candidate = np.rint(np.clip(candidate_raw,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
stress = np.rint(np.clip(stress_raw,0,255)).astype(np.uint8)
fractions = [float(np.mean((x < 0) | (x > 255))) for x in [candidate_raw, stress_raw]]
fig = panels([image, candidate, stress], ["Original", f"Candidate: clipped {fractions[0]:.1%}", f"Stress only: clipped {fractions[1]:.1%}"])

Read the result

The stress panel demonstrates failure modes without becoming an endorsed augmentation. Compare letters, rim and body shading, and relate the missing evidence to the stated label. Numeric legality alone cannot establish semantic validity.

Change and compare

  • Replay the candidate from parameters without another random draw.
  • Define a separate admissible policy for a color-recognition task and justify its restrictions.
